entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9341"/><div sID="gen16068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9341"/><hi type="bold">4. Surely ... our griefs--</hi>literally, "But yet He hath taken (or borne) our sicknesses," that is, they who despised Him because of His human infirmities ought rather to have esteemed Him on account of them; for thereby "Himself took OUR infirmities" (bodily diseases). So <reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Mt 8:17</reference> quotes it. In the Hebrew for "borne," or took, there is probably the double notion, He took on Himself vicariously (so <reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">Is 53:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">6, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">12</reference>), and so He took away; His perfect humanity whereby He was bodily afflicted for us, and in all our afflictions (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.15">He 4:15</reference>) was the ground on which He cured the sick; so that Matthew's quotation is not a mere accommodation. See Note 42 of Archbishop Magee, Atonement. The Hebrew there may mean to overwhelm with darkness; Messiah's time of darkness was temporary (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.45">Mt 27:45</reference>), answering to the bruising of His heel; Satan's is to be eternal, answering to the bruising of his head (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Is 50:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carried ... sorrows--</hi>The notion of substitution strictly. "Carried," namely, as a burden. "Sorrows," that is, pains of the mind; as "griefs" refer to pains of the body (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">Psa 32:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">38:17</reference>). <reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Mt 8:17</reference> might seem to oppose this: "And bare our sicknesses." But he uses "sicknesses" figuratively for sins, the cause of them. Christ took on Himself all man's "infirmities;" so as to remove them; the bodily by direct miracle, grounded on His participation in human infirmities; those of the soul by His vicarious suffering, which did away with the source of both. Sin and sickness are ethically connected as cause and effect (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Is 33:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Mt 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.14">Joh 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.15">Jas 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen16069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we did esteem him stricken--</hi>judicially [Lowth], namely, for His sins; whereas it was for ours. "We thought Him to be a leper" [Jerome, Vulgate], leprosy being the direct divine judgment for guilt (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.1-Lev.13.59">Le 13:1-59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.10">Nu 12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.12.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.18-2Chr.26.21">2Ch 26:18-21</reference>).<div eID="gen16070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smitten--</hi>by divine judgments.<div eID="gen16071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afflicted--</hi>for His sins; this was the point in which they so erred (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Lu 23:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">Ac 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>). He was, it is true, "afflicted," but not for His sins. <div eID="gen16072" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 53 Is 53:1-12 . Man's Unbelief: Messiah's Vicarious Sufferings, and Final Triumph for Man. The speaker, according to Horsley, personates the repenting Jews in the latter ages of the world coming over to the faith of the Redeemer; the whole is their penitent confession. This view suits the context ( Is 52:7-9 ), which is not to be fully realized until Israel is restored. However, primarily, it is the abrupt exclamation of the prophet: "Who hath believed our report," that of Isaiah and the other prophets, as to Messiah? The infidel's objection from the unbelief of the Jews is anticipated and hereby answered: that unbelief and the cause of it (Messiah's humiliation, whereas they looked for One coming to reign) were foreseen and foretold.
